clue.text: Written by Dr Watson in or out, of practice ?

definitions.text: Written by Dr Watson in or out, of practice ?

parts.words: Written by Dr Watson in or out, of practice
parts.note: Watson kept a record of Holmes's investigations, and as a medical man in practice he would also keep a register of his patients

explanation.surface: A question about what Sherlock Holmes's companion wrote, whether working as a doctor or not.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses fit Watson: the chronicle of Holmes's detective work, and the doctor's register of patients he kept while in medical practice.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's or detective's record of individual matters handled is such a book, and Watson wrote both kinds.

clue.text: Add crusty pastry all over

definitions.meaning: to put a crust on it, read as three words
from head to foot, a French-derived phrase used of armour

explanation.surface: An instruction in a recipe to cover something entirely with pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase, meaning from head to foot (as of a knight armed all over), splits into CAP A PIE: put a top on a pie.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means from head to foot, so completely, all over the body.

clue.text: Be patient, and, you may get on to it.

definitions.text: Be patient, and, you may get on to it.

parts.words: Be patient, and, you may get on to it.
parts.note: patient is not a call to wait but a noun: be a hospital patient and you may be carried on this

explanation.surface: Advice that waiting will eventually let you get onto something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be patient' reads as 'wait', but it means be a patient: an injured person is laid on this to be carried.
explanation.definitionFit: A hospital patient may be carried on this frame with handles, a litter for the injured.

clue.text: Mars with second-rate illuminations.

parts.note: second-class things are graded B
illuminations are lights

explanation.surface: The red planet seen with inferior lighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mars' is not the planet but a verb: spoils.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil or ruin something is to mar it, as a plant disease does.

clue.text: Choice bargains in the City

definitions.meaning: a range of things to pick from
the City is London's financial district, where contracts giving a right to buy or sell later at a set price are traded

explanation.surface: Selected cheap deals in London's financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district; there these are contracts giving the right to buy or sell shares at a fixed price later.
explanation.definitionFit: Alternatives to pick from are choices, and in finance the word names rights to buy or sell at a set price.

clue.text: The time of the year for jumpers?

definitions.text: The time of the year for jumpers?

parts.words: The time of the year for jumpers
parts.note: jumpers here are not sweaters but things that leap, and the season is named after a leap

explanation.surface: A question about which season suits wearing woolly sweaters.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'jumper' is British for a sweater, which suggests cold weather; but read it as 'one who jumps' and the season named for a leap fits.
explanation.definitionFit: The season after winter shares its name with a bound or leap, the thing jumpers do.

clue.text: Used by a draughtsman, to make a crossword ?

definitions.meaning: a draughtsman draws right angles with a triangular drawing instrument
a crossword setter would set a square grid

explanation.surface: An instrument a designer uses to build a crossword grid.
explanation.walkthrough: A draughtsman's triangular ruler for right angles; split, SET SQUARE describes compiling a square crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: The triangular drafting tool gives right angles; a compiler sets a puzzle whose grid is a square.

clue.text: Paradoxically, they appear to put an end, to noise

definitions.text: Paradoxically, they appear to put an end, to noise

parts.words: Paradoxically, they appear to put an end, to noise
parts.note: split in two, the name of these noisy people reads as a quarrel or din that ends, though they cause noise

explanation.surface: People who seem to silence noise, though the opposite is true.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as ROW DIES, the word says a din ends, which is the paradox: these troublemakers make the noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough, noisy, disorderly people make a din rather than ending one.

clue.text: She was irked by a double negative

definitions.text: She was irked by a double negative

parts.words: She was irked by a double negative
parts.note: a 1925 musical comedy's title puts two noes before a girl's name

explanation.surface: A woman annoyed by a grammatical error.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical 'No, No, Nanette' (1925) has a double negative in its title before the heroine's name, so she is the one told no twice.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the musical 'No, No, ...' is a girl addressed with two refusals.

clue.text: Under torture ten 'priests are not giving up

indicators.note: letters under torture are twisted and wrenched out of shape, so the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Clergymen being tortured refuse to recant their faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under torture' twists the ten letters of TEN PRIESTS into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who keeps going without surrendering is dogged and unrelenting.

clue.text: Flies above the' stage-with this on either side

definitions.text: Flies above the' stage-with this on either side

parts.words: Flies above the' stage-with this on either side
parts.note: in a theatre the flies are the space above the stage, and the areas off to left and right have their own name

explanation.surface: Insects buzz over a theatre stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flies' looks like insects or a verb, but it is the theatre term for the loft above the stage; the offstage spaces at its sides are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre's side area, out of the audience's view, is so called, like a bird's side limb.

clue.text: A random design for cover on retirement

definitions.text: A random design for cover on retirement

parts.words: A random design for cover on retirement
parts.note: retirement here means going to bed at night, and the cover is a bedspread made of assorted pieces

explanation.surface: Sounds like an arbitrary insurance scheme for someone leaving work with a pension.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover on retirement' suggests pension insurance; retirement is going to bed, and the cover is a bedspread sewn from random scraps.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedspread stitched from assorted fabric scraps has a haphazard design and covers you when you go to bed.

clue.text: Sheep scatter before us in the old town

indicators.note: sheep scatter when a flock breaks up, so the letters of the word are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A flock disperses ahead of us in an ancient settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scatter' is the anagram signal on the first word. Ephesus was an ancient Greek city on the coast of what is now Turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: This ruined city of Asia Minor, addressed in one of Paul's epistles, is an ancient settlement.

clue.text: Advantage of being a superior workman?

definitions.meaning: a position of control over an opponent
upper means superior and a hand is a worker

explanation.surface: The benefit of being an expert craftsman.
explanation.walkthrough: A hand is a manual worker, so a superior one is an 'upper' hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Control or a dominant position is an advantage; a hand is a labourer, so an upper one is a higher-ranked worker.

clue.text: They are in at opposite ends of a chain

definitions.text: They are in at opposite ends of a chain

parts.words: They are in at opposite ends of a chain
parts.note: a chain is an old measure of 22 yards, the length of a cricket pitch, and two players are in, one at each end

explanation.surface: People positioned at either end of a linked chain.
explanation.walkthrough: A chain is 22 yards, the length of a cricket pitch; in cricket the two players 'in' (currently batting) stand at its opposite ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Two cricket players who are in stand at the two ends of the pitch, which measures one chain.

clue.text: Innocent result of the Mikado's penal reforms

definitions.text: Innocent result of the Mikado's penal reforms

parts.words: Innocent result of the Mikado's penal reforms
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's Mikado, making each punishment fit the crime is called a source of innocent fun

explanation.surface: Sounds like a judgement on a Japanese ruler's prison reforms.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Mikado the emperor sings of making the punishment fit the crime, calling it 'a source of innocent merriment'.
explanation.definitionFit: The emperor's song names harmless fun and jollity as what his fitting punishments produce.

clue.text: A tenacious old Roman general?

parts.note: a tenacious person is one who holds tight, a gripper, and a Roman commander's name sounds like that phrase

explanation.surface: Describes a stubborn military leader of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman general Marcus Agrippa, Augustus's commander, has a name that sounds like 'a gripper', someone tenacious.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa was the Roman admiral and commander who won at Actium for Augustus.

clue.text: It is issued for light service

definitions.text: It is issued for light service

parts.words: It is issued for light service
parts.note: light service sounds like easy duty, but it is the supply of fuel for lamps and the demand for payment sent out

explanation.surface: An order for undemanding duty is handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light service' suggests easy duties; it is the supply of fuel that once lit homes, for which a utility issues a demand for payment.
explanation.definitionFit: A utility sends this payment demand for the fuel supply that once powered domestic lamps.

clue.text: A journalist doesn't exercise self-denial to create an effect

parts.note: a reporter who does not deny who they are says 'I am the press', contracted

explanation.surface: A reporter shows off to make a mark.
explanation.walkthrough: A journalist who does not deny themself would say 'I'm press', which read as one word means to make a strong effect.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a strong mark on someone's mind is to impress them, producing an effect.

clue.text: Unnecessary exhortation to Kate to curse

definitions.meaning: Kate in Shakespeare's Taming of the Shrew is already a scold, so urging her to be one is needless
an archaic verb meaning to wish evil on

explanation.surface: Telling Kate to do something pointless, and to swear.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as BE SHREW, it urges Katherina of The Taming of the Shrew to be what she already is; as one word it is an old verb for curse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespearean oath 'beshrew me' wishes ill on oneself, so the word means damn; split, it tells Kate to act like a scold.

clue.text: A feast, for deflationists?

definitions.meaning: deflationists let the air out of things, so a tyre puncture suits them

explanation.surface: A banquet for economists who favour lowering prices.
explanation.walkthrough: Deflationists suggests economists; here it is people letting air out, as in a burst tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge meal is a slap-up feed, and a burst tyre releases its air, deflating it.

clue.text: The surgeon holds 'fifty places, roughly

indicators.note: roughly means approximately or carelessly, so the letters are arranged in rough fashion

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A doctor has fifty jobs, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' shuffles L (fifty) with PLACES. 'Holds' is not a container sign: the definition is what the surgeon holds.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon grips this small sharp knife when operating.

clue.text: Successful sportsmen point to target scores

parts.note: W, west, is a compass point
in archery and shooting, hits in the ring next to the bull are called inners

explanation.surface: Victorious athletes aim at what they score.
explanation.walkthrough: W is a compass point; an inner is a shot in the ring just outside the bullseye of a target.
explanation.definitionFit: Victors in sporting contests come first, so they are victorious players.

clue.text: Religious overwork ?

parts.note: in theology, good works done beyond what God requires are called by a special Latin-derived term

explanation.surface: A complaint about doing too much churchgoing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Catholic theology this is the performance of good works beyond what duty requires, which builds up merit.
explanation.definitionFit: The theological term names doing more than duty demands, so it is work beyond the required amount.

clue.text: Is prudent when we put about

indicators.note: the word we is put about, around, the other piece, so it contains it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that it is sensible for us to change course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put about' sounds like a ship changing tack, but here it means placed around: one piece encloses the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Sensible and judicious people show sound judgement, which is being prudent.

clue.text: Anyhow here's to Pam-the all-rounder !

indicators.note: done anyhow means done in a careless jumble, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A toast raised to Pam, who is good at everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyhow' rearranges HERESTOPAM. An all-rounder in cricket bats and bowls, but here it is what surrounds everything: the air around the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The envelope of gases encircles the whole globe, so it goes all round it.

clue.text: Like the shop for half the three-day: week ?

definitions.text: Like the shop for half the three-day: week ?

parts.words: Like the shop for half the three-day: week
parts.note: the three-day week of 1974 limited businesses to three days' power, but read as half of a normal week, the shop is shut

explanation.surface: A question about shops during Britain's three-day week of power cuts in 1974.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain's 1974 three-day week let firms use electricity only three days a week; a six-day trading week cut to three means the shop is not open for half of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop not open for trading is shut, as it was for half the usual week.

clue.text: Old columnists given to asceticism

parts.note: columnists here are not journalists but hermits who lived on top of columns as a religious discipline

explanation.surface: Veteran newspaper writers who lead self-denying lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Columnists' suggests journalists, but these are early Christian ascetics, like Simeon, who lived atop pillars.
explanation.definitionFit: Early Christian hermits who lived atop pillars practised extreme self-denial, so they were old ascetics on columns.
